beliefs.practice: Create and reuse a single Motor/MongoClient instance (singleton) for the whole FastAPI process and set an explicit connection pool size (e.g. maxPoolSize) rather than opening a new client per request.

Keep the DOCUMENTDB_URI out of source control: read the connection string from environment or a secrets store and use Azure Key Vault / Managed Identity in production rather than embedding credentials in code or files.
Require TLS/SSL for the MongoDB connection and validate certificates (do not disable certificate verification in production).

Set explicit readConcern/readPreference and writeConcern appropriate to your durability/latency needs (e.g. w=majority for stronger durability or w=1 for lower latency) and test behavior under expected failure modes.

Implement idempotent retries with exponential backoff for transient errors and use driver's retryWrites (and retryable reads) where supported; handle DuplicateKey and other non-idempotent errors explicitly instead of blind retries.

Create a compound index matching query and window partition/sort patterns — for moving-average queries use an index like { patientId: 1, testCode: 1, timestamp: 1 } so partitionBy=patientId,testCode and sortBy=timestamp can use the index.
Use a TTL index on the timestamp field (or collection-level TTL) to automatically expire old time-series data according to retention requirements instead of manual deletes.

For high-ingest time-series data consider a bucketed document model (e.g., one document per patient/test/hour with an array of measurements) instead of one-document-per-measurement to reduce index pressure and RU consumption; only use raw-per-sample if ingestion rate is moderate.

When using $setWindowFields for moving averages, partition and sort exactly as your index is ordered, and include allowDiskUse in heavy aggregations; push $match/$sort before window stages when possible to reduce working set.

Use change streams for real-time alerts but persist resume tokens and implement robust resume logic (handle resumable errors and full resync) so the listener can recover from restarts and transient errors.
Keep change-stream listeners single-threaded per resume token and checkpoint progress (e.g., write resume tokens to durable storage periodically) to avoid losing events on process crashes.

Precompute and store boolean flags used for alerting (e.g., isCritical, isOutOfRange) and add an index on those flags when you need fast queries for alerts, instead of scanning recent documents each time.
Provision RU/s (or enable autoscale) sized to handle ingestion spikes and aggregation workloads; design the partition key and throttling strategy so hot partitions don’t cause RU storms.

Choose a partition key with high cardinality and even distribution (candidate: patientId or patientId_testCode) to avoid hotspots for time-series insert-heavy workloads; test with representative load.
Monitor RU consumption, index usage, operation latency, and change-stream errors with the provider's monitoring tools and set alerts for sustained throttling or long-running aggregations.
Create indexes during low-traffic windows or use background index builds if supported; be aware index builds can temporarily increase RU and storage costs and may impact writes.
Use Beanie Pydantic models and enforce schema validation (server-side JSON schema or app-level validation) so documents always include patientId, testCode, value, timestamp with correct types.
Avoid multi-partition transactions for high-throughput time-series ingestion; if you need transactions, limit them to single-partition operations and keep transactions short.

If using vector fields and the cluster's vector indexes, store normalized vectors in a dedicated field and configure the vector index parameters (index type HNSW/IVF, efConstruction, m, etc.) appropriate to your recall/latency tradeoff — and limit vector dimensionality and document size.
Do not rely on TTL as the only protection—use provider backups and a retention policy so you can recover deleted or expired data when needed.
Restrict network access to the database with IP firewall rules or VNet integration and grant the application least-privilege MongoDB users/roles instead of using full-admin credentials.
Use allowDiskUse: true for memory-heavy aggregations and paginate aggregation windows (or pre-aggregate) to keep working set and RU usage reasonable.

Make seed and demo scripts idempotent: use upsert or delete/insert patterns and avoid writing production credentials into scripts; include an environment-based guard to prevent accidental runs against non-sample DBs.

Verify driver and server feature compatibility: ensure Motor/PyMongo versions and the cluster's MongoDB wire protocol version support features you use (e.g., $setWindowFields, change streams), and fail fast if incompatible.

Log operational events (index creation, aggregation plans/explain when debugging, change-stream errors) but never log secrets; capture slow-query samples and use explain() to verify critical queries use the intended index.
